The table reports mIoU, cIoU/oIoU, and precision-at-threshold metrics (Pr@50–Pr@90). Fig. 11: Visualization of language-guided temporal attention and mask decoding. The decoder [SEG] attention maps concentrate on the regions described by the referring expressions, and the intermediate query masks progressively localize the target changed objects before producing the final prediction.

Fig. 10: Qualitative comparisons on the RS domain. We compare our method with representative LVLM baselines on remote-sensing multi-temporal referring segmentation. The results show that our method can better capture building-level and region-level temporal changes under aerial-view scenes, producing masks that are more consistent with the ground truth.

Fig. 2: From single-time language-guided segmentation to multi-temporal referring segmentation. Complementary to the task motivation in Figure 1, this figure summarizes the evolution of segmentation tasks from both textual and visual complexity. From the textual perspective, language-guided segmentation evolves from category-level open-vocabulary segmentation, to instance-level referring segmentation, and further to reasoning segmentation with implicit semantic understanding. From the visual perspective, MTRS introduces an additional temporal dimension, requiring models to compare temporally related images and segment the language-specified change rather than a static object. This motivates the construction of MTRefSeg-21K and the design of a change-aware LVLM framework for language-grounded temporal change segmentation.

Fig. 9: Qualitative comparisons on the NS domain. We compare our method with representative LVLM baselines under normal-scene multi-temporal referring segmentation. The examples cover object disappearance, appearance, and state changes. Compared with existing LVLMs, our method produces more complete and spatially accurate masks that better match the language-specified temporal changes.

Fig. 8: Overview of the proposed MTRefSeg-R1 framework. MTRefSeg-R1 adopts a two-stage training strategy. Stage 1 performs multi-temporal vision pretraining on diverse view types to learn generic change-aware visual representations. Stage 2 conducts referring multi-temporal fine-tuning, where the LVLM understands temporally ordered image pairs and language instructions, and predicts the mask of the referred changed region through the [SEG] token and the change-aware mask decoder.

Fig. 3: Overview of CRAFT-Agent. CRAFT-Agent constructs bi-image–text–mask triplets for MTRS by integrating grid-aware change perception, expression generation, mask refinement, expression beautification, and human auditing.

TABLE VII: Comparison of different methods under the RS domain setting, where models are trained and evaluated within the remote-sensing domain. This setting evaluates in-domain performance on remote-sensing change referring segmentation, where the training and validation data share similar aerial-view appearance, object scale, and spatial layout distributions.

TABLE IV: Quantitative comparison results on MTRefSeg21K in terms of mean performance. We report the mean performance across the Train→Val, NS→NS, and RS→RS settings, including mIoU, cIoU/oIoU, and Pr@50. Best results in each column are highlighted in bold.
Fig. 4: Data design for MTRS. MTRefSeg-21K provides fine-grained bi-image–text–mask triplets for language-guided multi-temporal referring fine-tuning across RS and NS domains.
